problems.title: Utilisation
problems.statement: One execution unit, one instruction per cycle. Each thread repeatedly does $C = 3$ cycles of work, then waits $L = 27$ cycles for a load. There are $N = 4$ threads.

parts.prompt: Threads needed to saturate the unit?

hints: Each thread needs C out of every C + L cycles.

problems.title: Realistic numbers
problems.statement: A streaming kernel does $C = 5$ cycles of work per load; memory latency is $L = 395$ cycles.

parts.prompt: Threads per execution unit to saturate it?

problems.solution: $\lceil 400/5 \rceil = 80$. With four schedulers per SM, that's 320 threads (10 warps) per SM just for this kernel to keep up: the scale GPUs are built for.

problems.title: Instruction-level parallelism
problems.statement: Now each thread issues $k = 4$ independent loads back to back, waits $L = 400$ cycles for all of them, then does $C = 4$ cycles of work per loaded value ($kC = 16$ cycles in all) before repeating.

parts.prompt: Threads needed to saturate the unit?
And with k = 1 (one load at a time)?

hints: A period is now kC + L, of which the unit is needed kC cycles.
problems.solution: (a) $kC + L = 16 + 400 = 416$. (b) $\lceil 416/16 \rceil = 26$. (c) $\lceil 404/4 \rceil = 101$. Four independent loads per thread cut the threads needed by almost 4× (not exactly: the work per period grew, but the latency didn't).

problems.title: From registers to utilisation
problems.statement: An SM has 65,536 registers, 4 warp schedulers and a limit of 64 warps. A kernel uses 40 registers per thread (registers are allocated per warp: 32 × 40). Per load, a warp does $C = 8$ cycles of issue; memory latency is $L = 400$.
hints: Each scheduler is its own execution unit with its share of the warps.
problems.solution: (a) $\lfloor 65536 / 1280 \rfloor = 51$ warps. (b) $51/4 = 12.75$. (c) $12.75 \times 8 / 408 = 25\%$. A scheduler needs $\lceil 408/8 \rceil = 51$ warps to saturate, four times what it has. The fix is either fewer registers (more warps) or more independent loads per warp (more ILP).

problems.title: When registers stop mattering
problems.statement: Same SM: 65,536 registers, at most 64 warps (2,048 threads).

parts.prompt: Warps resident at 24 registers per thread?

hints: One register over 32 costs whole warps.
problems.solution: (a) $65536/(32\times24) = 85.3$, capped at 64: full occupancy. (b) $\lfloor 65536/1056 \rfloor = 62$. (c) $62/64 = 96.9\%$. The cliff edges in occupancy come from integer division; Part 2's occupancy chapter adds the finer granularity real GPUs use.

problems.title: How long does the whole job take?
problems.statement: One execution unit processes 1,000,000 items. Each item is a load (latency 400) followed by 4 cycles of work. 64 threads share the items.
hints: The unit must spend 4 × 10⁶ cycles on work. Divide by utilisation.
With enough threads, the unit is saturated and only the work counts.
problems.solution: (a) $\min(1, 64 \times 4/404) = 63.4\%$. (b) Work is $4\times10^6$ cycles; at 63.4% busy that's $4\times10^6 \times 404/256 = 6{,}312{,}500$ cycles. Equivalently, each thread finishes an item every 404 cycles, so 64 threads do $64/404$ items per cycle. (c) 128 threads exceed $N_{sat} = 101$, so the unit is saturated: $4\times10^6$ cycles. Doubling the threads made it 1.58× faster, not 2×: past saturation, extra threads buy nothing.

problems.title: What latency hiding doesn't do
problems.statement: You add more threads to a latency-bound kernel and it gets faster.

parts.prompt: What happened to the latency of each individual load?
options: It stayed the same (or rose slightly under load): it's hidden, not shortened

parts.prompt: What happened to each individual thread's run time?
options: It stayed about the same or grew: threads share the unit

problems.solution: Multithreading improves the unit's throughput by overlapping waits. Each load still takes as long (more, if memory gets busier: Chapter 0.1's loaded latency), and each thread takes at least as long, since it now shares the unit. This is the defining trade of throughput machines.

problems.title: Uneven phases
problems.statement: A thread repeatedly: loads (latency 400), does 2 cycles of work, does a dependent load (latency 400), then does 6 cycles of work.
hints: The utilisation formula holds with C = total work per period and L = total waiting per period.
Dependent loads can't overlap with each other.
problems.solution: (a) $2 + 6 = 8$. (b) $8 + 400 + 400 = 808$. (c) $\lceil 808/8 \rceil = 101$. The general rule: $N_{sat} = \lceil (\text{work} + \text{wait}) / \text{work} \rceil$ per period, whatever the shape of the period, as long as all threads behave alike and the scheduler never idles while a thread is ready.

problems.title: Why SMT isn't enough on a CPU
problems.statement: A CPU core runs 2 hardware threads (SMT). On a memory-bound loop each thread does 20 cycles of work per DRAM miss of 300 cycles, and can't overlap misses.

parts.prompt: Hardware threads needed to saturate the core?

hints: Same formula as a GPU scheduler.
problems.solution: (a) $2 \times 20/320 = 12.5\%$. (b) $\lceil 320/20 \rceil = 16$. Each extra hardware thread needs a full copy of the architectural registers and more bookkeeping; CPUs stop at 2 (sometimes 4 or 8) because their per-thread state is large. GPUs keep per-thread state small (no big out-of-order machinery) so that dozens of warps fit.

problems.title: The GW-1 at full scale
problems.statement: Treat each GW-1 SM as one execution unit issuing one warp instruction per cycle, memory latency 400 cycles, at most 64 resident warps. A kernel issues $C = 6$ instructions per load per warp.

parts.prompt: Utilisation with 64 warps per SM, in %?
Utilisation if registers limit it to 24 warps, in %?
Warps needed to saturate (compare with the 64-warp limit)?
With 64 warps, the minimum independent loads per warp (k) to saturate?

hints: With k loads in flight per warp, the period is kC + L and the work is kC.
Solve 64 · kC ≥ kC + L for the smallest integer k.
problems.solution: (a) $64 \times 6 / 406 = 94.6\%$. (b) $24 \times 6/406 = 35.5\%$. (c) $\lceil 406/6 \rceil = 68 > 64$: thread-level parallelism alone can't saturate this SM. (d) $64 \cdot 6k \ge 6k + 400 \Rightarrow 378k \ge 400 \Rightarrow k \ge 1.06$, so $k = 2$. When occupancy runs out, ILP is the only lever left: the central idea of Volkov's paper in Part 2.
